topic: Göy niyə mavidir (Why is the sky blue)
research_summary: The well-known answer (Rayleigh scattering) is only half the story: air scatters violet even more than blue (~9.4x vs red at 400 vs 700 nm), yet we see blue because the Sun emits less violet, some is absorbed high up, and our eye cones respond to the violet+blue mix like 'blue plus white'. No Azerbaijani-language animated explainer was found — a clear gap.

data_points.claim: Rayleigh scattering is proportional to 1/wavelength^4; blue (450 nm) scatters ~4.3x more than red (650 nm)
Violet (400 nm) scatters ~9.4x more than red (700 nm) — yet the sky isn't violet
Skylight spectrum is about equal parts violet and blue; eyes perceive it as blue plus white (Glenn Smith, American Journal of Physics)
Tyndall (1859) observed blue scattering; Rayleigh quantified it in 1871; Einstein settled molecular scattering in 1911
Moon's sky is black — no atmosphere to scatter light
Mars: butterscotch daytime sky, blue sunsets (Curiosity, April 2015)
Red sunsets: sunlight crosses much thicker air at low sun angles, blue is scattered out

common_questions: Why isn't it violet if violet scatters more?
Is the sky blue because it reflects the ocean?

misconceptions.myth: The sky is blue because it reflects the ocean
misconceptions.reality: Sky blue comes from scattering by N2/O2 molecules; the ocean is blue mainly because water absorbs red
Violet scatters even more; our eyes and the solar spectrum make it look blue

audience_insights.knowledge_level: General Azerbaijani-speaking audience; many have heard 'light scattering' but not why it's not violet
